heard: you can see one impossible galaxy through the gap of another. In 1950, Arthur Hoge found a blue smoke ring around a golden core in the Serpents constellation. Hoge first thought this bizarre structure was a simple planetary nebula or a gas cloud. He even guessed it was an optical illusion caused by gravity-bending distant light. But Hoge's object is a real galaxy, 600 million light years away and wider than the Milky Way. Most ring galaxies form from violent collisions, yet no crash site exists here. Peering through the dark gap at the one o'clock position reveals a one-in-a-million photobomb. Deep in the background sits another ring galaxy, perfectly aligned with the first. It is the only place where you can see one impossible galaxy through the gap of another.
